claims: The Jones Act (Merchant Marine Act of 1920) is a federal statute.
The Jones Act requires that all goods transported by water between U.S. ports be carried on ships that are U.S.-flagged.
The Jones Act requires that all goods transported by water between U.S. ports be carried on U.S.-built ships.
The Jones Act requires that all goods transported by water between U.S. ports be carried on ships owned by U.S. citizens.
The Jones Act requires that all goods transported by water between U.S. ports be carried on ships crewed by U.S. citizens.
The Jones Act was enacted post-World War I.
The Jones Act applies to shipping between U.S. ports, including noncontiguous states and territories like Hawaii, Alaska, and Puerto Rico.
The Jones Act provides a legal framework for sailors to seek damages for injuries caused by employer negligence.
The Department of Homeland Security can temporarily waive the Jones Act in the interest of national defense.
Jones Act waivers are often used to address fuel shortages.
Maritime unions strongly support the Jones Act.
The U.S. Coast Guard strongly supports the Jones Act.
The Jones Act supports roughly 500,000 jobs.
The Jones Act supports $29 billion in wages.
Critics argue the Jones Act limits shipping options.
Critics argue the Jones Act increases costs for consumers, especially in Hawaii and Puerto Rico.
Critics argue the Jones Act hinders energy efficiency.
